utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, sir, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dodaj, good morning.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We will continue where we left off yesterday. If you will recall, we talked about the position where your unit was before you surrendered. From the description that you gave here in these proceedings, and you will tell me if I am right or not, it seems right in front of you you did not have or you did not see any enemy soldiers, if I can call them that. What you saw were houses, mostly empty houses which you entered occasionally to take various items, such as underwear?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the day you decided and agreed with your mates to surrender, was that the direction you took to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You left in uniforms and you all had weapons.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The three other soldiers whom you saw later in the police station, Kuscevic, Kobas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the third name the interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: They were there in that area that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just to repeat for the transcript, I will repeat the names. One is Kuscevic, the second one is Rasid, and the third one is Kobas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how it could have happened that on that same day those three soldiers were arrested, probably in that same area that you passed without any problems and you asked, as you explained, to be brought in touch with the ZNG there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how it happened that they came to be captured?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody lived in those houses. There were cases that people from MUP came to those houses, and some soldiers came at that point. Perhaps soldiers entered those houses and the police officers came at the same time and that's how they were captured. Probably the soldiers did not put any -- up any resistance, and that's how they were captured, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the MUP, you mean the MUP from Croatia, MUP from Croatia, from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the MUP from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you said, is that something that you assume or is that something that you heard?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they told me. I don't know how true that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, when you were talking about the order to open fire as a response to fire from the other side, and that it used to happen that fire was opened not only because of incoming fire, but because of noises, you mentioned the rustling of corn-stalks and other sounds, because of which you opened fire on your side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can that mean that your assertion that fire was opened constantly day and night is not true? I'm speaking about your unit.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, fire was opened on a daily basis. It wasn't being done from minute to minute. Five to six times a day we fired. At night there were more fierce attacks. There was more firing, firing from tanks, from armoured vehicles, from infantry weapons. At night we didn't see anybody coming towards us or hear anything, but you could hear the rustling. And sometimes in the dark if you were looking in one single direction, then the image would shift. This would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In front of the tanks and the armoured vehicles there was a space that wasn't guarded in any other way other than the tanks, the transporters, the armoured vehicles, and you who were securing that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it would have happen, especially at night, that there would be more fire, more because of a fear of an attack from that side or in order to prevent an attack?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was probably opened out of fear, because in Sremska Mitrovica they kept harping on about how there were 20.000 Ustashas in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you believe that especially at night there was a danger of an attack being carried out?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't believe that. I knew that nobody would attack us or that anybody would come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were not personally present and were not able to hear the orders, do you know if in front of you or from any side there were JNA units or some other units that were moving to the centre of Vukovar and this fire of yours was supposed to cover them in some way? You know what I'm talking about, to strike at positions in front of them?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no JNA units in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, not immediately from what you said, but further along in Vukovar, yes?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe from some other side, but not directly in front of us, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if fire was opened without any targeting positions of those who were in Vukovar and were attacking Vukovar and going from street to street would also be in danger of being hit, since we heard from witnesses that there was a house-to-house combat and fighting for each house?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want me to say to that. I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. We won't press on that, because you were not able to hear the orders directly, but you did say something about that. The order to your unit, was it to control the Vukovar-Vinkovci road, that axis, and to prevent any transport and to open fire if it was in danger or attacked?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sir, we cut off that road so nobody used that road anymore. We were not controlling the road. What I'm talking about is that there was shooting at the town without any control. We were not hitting any police lines or positions of the ZNG. We were hitting the entire town of Vukovar. There were houses in front of us. JNA officers by day would climb on a tree and they would hit Bogdanovci out of snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that you cut off the road, does that mean -- well, you say that nobody appeared. Had somebody appeared, you had orders to act, didn't you, because that was why that unit was there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we probably would have opened fire at those people, regardless of whether they were civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about incoming fire in relation to you, I think that you said that only once it happened that there was a mortar attack and that was when the captain and another soldier was seriously, wounded and I think that you said that this happened on the 17th of September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't really tell you exactly what date, but it was sometime between the 14th and the 16th of September. There were four mortar shells that hit our position. It was in the middle of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were talking about the 14th and the 17th or that period, I think you said that that was the period of the fiercest attacks by the JNA, and that up to the 14th there were no such attacks, and then after the 14th they lasted for several days?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there were no such strong attacks. They also used airplanes to strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it means that during those days, during the fiercest fighting and the attacks using artillery and even airplanes as you say against Vukovar, that was when this mortar attack on your positions occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe that four mortars were sent to our positions and then we hit back with over 100 mortars back, I don't know what sort of an attack you're talking about. Had we not been there, nobody would have attacked. Had we stayed in the barracks, nobody would have attacked us, probably, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope that we're understanding each other properly, that these four shells dropped, hit your positions as you said. And you say that these were the only shells during that entire time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the 24-day period, these were the only shells that fell at our positions. This is something that I guarantee. I have no reason to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely one of my questions. Is it logical that only that one single time your position was hit by mortars during the time when the fiercest attacks were being carried out against the other side and then, as you claim, there were no other attacks after that. Are you saying this because that -- there is evidence that the captain was seriously wounded that day, and that's why you're only talking about that day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody is shelling the town with airplanes, I don't know which soldiers would fire back at that very instance, especially soldiers who did not have the proper weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned the airplanes, I think that you said - and I'm asking you whether this was on the 14th of September - that you saw the airplanes in action over Vukovar for the first time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw planes before, but between the 14th and the 16th and the 17th they were really rocketing the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That is exactly what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come down from Negoslavci and hit the town.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please pause between answer and question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise because of the transcript it wasn't recorded precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that then between the 14th and the 17th you saw planes in action, they were shelling, and then before that you saw on some other days that the planes were just flying over?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were flying over and then they would fire the occasional shell. But between the 14th and the 16th they were really using all available means to shell the town. The whole town was burning. There was a cloud of smoke in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, you must admit that you were quite far from the town. That's how you described the positions and explained it on the map.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far that was in kilometres, but there was smoke in front of us and you could see the water-tower in front of us very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you sure that from the position where you were dug in with your unit you were able to see the water-tower?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we did hit the water-tower, not once but several times, because there was a Croatian flag flying on the water-tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is there an elevation, you know what I mean, a hill between the positions where you were and Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to you, the terrain is straight and flat and there were no elevations or anything that could impede the view of the water-tower from there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was all flat and visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about it yesterday, and you also mentioned it earlier, that during the attacks, during those days that you're talking about, three civilians surrendered?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is: How did you conclude that these were civilians when you said about one of them that he was carrying a Kalashnikov? Is that because they wore civilian clothing or was there some other reason, since at least one of them was armed and he had a weapon such as a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians. They were probably civilians. They were not soldiers; they were not wearing uniforms. They did have Kalashnikov; they did have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you made that assessment based on the fact that they wore civilian clothes. My question is: Those who called themselves the defenders of Vukovar, did they all have uniforms. Or was it not the case that the majority did not have uniforms and wore their own civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had uniforms, some wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that just because they wore civilian clothes does not mean that they were civilians. They could also have been fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as whether they were fighting in Vukovar, if they were fighting, why were they fleeing from Vukovar? They surrendered to the army, to the soldiers, because they believed that the JNA would save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: For the record, let us repeat. You said that some of those who were involved in the Home Guards Corps wore uniforms, others didn't and wore their civilian clothes in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of the three that you said were later taken to Negoslavci, you mentioned that you had heard later at the police station that the three men had been killed. How come that you were able to hear that in Vukovar if all that happened in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I ran away from the JNA, when I came to the police, I told the policemen that three civilians had surrendered to the army, that they were tied, and remained overnight bound, that the mosquitos bit them all over, and the policemen told me that two of them had been killed, whereas the third one had been -- had been put on a cross, on a train carriage, and then killed with a tank grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have to wait. How were those people in Vukovar able to know that it was precisely those three that had been killed in the way you describe? There were many incidents, many people must have surrendered?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I told them that they were running towards our positions, where I was, in order to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But they were not killed in Vukovar. You said yourself that they had been taken to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guarantee they're not alive. You should take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's your assumption, you don't have any proof of that, do you? When you surrendered, as you describe, you said you spent three days at the police station practically in detention while you were being vetted, together with the other three soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that vetting, you obviously enjoyed the full confidence of those people, because they told you, as you testified yesterday, that you were free to do what you like, you could leave Vukovar or stay, although it later turned out that you couldn't, actually. You were not able to leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your opinion, and from what you saw that day and in the following days, did the defence of Vukovar have so many men that they didn't need people like you who were former soldiers, had adequate training, that they had such resources that they were able to dispense with you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that we deserted from that army and we were very young, I was 19, and we told them we wished to go towards Vinkovci, if we can get transport towards Zagreb, but they were not able to take us out of Vukovar because Vukovar was encircled. The three of us who joined the defence of Vukovar, it made no difference to their fate with or without us. There were only three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You are talking about the three of you, whereas the total number was seven or eight?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five surrendered and three were captured. Srecko Ravlija lost his leg. He was hit by a shell and he lost his leg and he remained back in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the days after you were released following the vetting when they trusted you. He didn't lose his leg then; it must have been later. At the moment I'm talking about, the decision was being made -- please wait for the end of the question. At the moment I'm talking about, the decision was being made whether you were going to join or you were going to leave. Was it logical, does it make sense for them to offer you freedom when you were trained soldiers and Croats rather than stay with them and fight, because in view of the losses they didn't -- they couldn't have had too many men?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning they did their very best to take us out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you probably knew, since you were in the unit that prevented any further communication along the road to Vukovar, you knew that it was impossible?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we thought that maybe some passage was possible still.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have a question for you personally. When you were making your choice about whether to surrender or not, was it motivated by the desire to leave the JNA and go home, or to leave the JNA and join the other side and fight on their side?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the army simply because I didn't want to be in that army, because I thought it was a criminal army committing an aggression. It wasn't our army. I left simply because I didn't see it as my army. And nobody forced me to join either the MUP or the defence of Vukovar. It was my choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You again failed to answer my question. What was your motivation? Yes, I understand you wanted to leave the army, but did you want to leave the army and go home or to join somebody else?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when I was running away, the idea was to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned, and I can refresh your memory, that precisely around that time on the 24th your unit was about to be replaced when you made your decision. Was that the decisive factor that pushed you to surrender?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the replacement was coming within days. I even think that people on those positions had been there for a little over a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that was the time when the replacement was about to occur, and your unit was going to leave that Vukovar front line anyway; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You knew that, but that didn't suit you. Wasn't that the -- an easier way to be done with the army, certainly easier than the way you chose to leave the army. Doesn't that demonstrate that your real desire was to join the other side in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My real wish was to leave that army as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that your colleague Dukana [as interpreted] was somewhere from Marinci from the surrounding area and that he was helpful because he was familiar with the terrain and he accompanied you. Dohanaj. If I am not mistaken, Marinci is very close to the positions where you were located but not facing Vukovar but on the other side?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you go towards Vinkovci, first comes Bogdanovci, then Marinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just let me check the transcript. So you said that it's Bogdanovci and then Marinci that come first. So it's around there. Didn't you decide to go towards Marinci because that must have been an easier way to leave the JNA, that's where his house and his family was?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had decided that way, that would have been more dangerous. It was easier to go towards Vukovar, then towards Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us go back to this police station where you spent some time. You said yourself that you had spent several days there, and you mentioned that it had its own prison, probably down there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also mentioned some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the time you spent there, and that for a while you were officially part of their police force, you must know who those people were and why they were kept prisoner?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in soldiers' uniforms. They were reservists, at least four of them were reservists, and there was one elderly woman with her husband, and I think her son was the JNA captain in the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's what you mentioned in your statements. I'm interested in knowing this: This elderly woman whom you believed to be the mother of some JNA captain who was in the barracks, why would that put her in jail? Because she was detained, as you said, together with her husband.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was safer for her to be on the premises of that prison than anywhere outside. And let me just tell you, they got the same food that the policemen ate, nobody touched a hair on their heads inside, they were not beaten, they got everything that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. What I really want to know is the reason why they, especially this elderly woman, should have been inside. Is that your assumption, or did you hear anybody saying that she was kept there to keep her safe?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just heard that one -- that her son was a JNA captain. In the end of all of them were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the end of which -- at the end of what?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the MUP building burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 15th, between the 13th and the 15th. I can't remember exactly which date it was. I think in November the MUP building burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it must have been a couple of days before the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that. Maybe seven, maybe 10 days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you hear or see or know about any other captive JNA members?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Nobody but the people you mentioned as being in the police station, you never heard or saw anyone else?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. Nobody apart from the four I mentioned, and this elderly woman with her husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of the hospital, you mentioned that there were three JNA members; one sergeant and two soldiers. I'm not going to deal with the hospital now, I'll come to it later, but they were certainly taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not held prisoner. They were at the hospital and they were undergoing treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But in order to reach the hospital in the surrounded Vukovar, they must have been taken prisoner and brought there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given assistance there, they were given treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course they were receiving treatment. We know that, we have information. But they arrived at the hospital as wounded captives, people who had been taken prisoner. Please, let us try not to interrupt each other. Let us observe a pause between question and answer, and you start answering when I finish my question. Since you later spoke about this, did you, during your day with the police, find out how they were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew they were at the hospital, I didn't know they were taken prisoner. I know there were negotiating with Raseta not to shell the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP men told us, because the policemen kept guard outside that room lest anybody came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean a policeman at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the ward where they were lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you heard at the police station that they were negotiating. When was that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that they were talking, the sergeant was talking to Raseta about the shelling of the hospital. I think this man was commander of the barracks in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please let me finish my question and don't interrupt me. You heard that at the police station, you cannot put a date on it, was it before the police station burnt down or later? Could that be a -- an indicator of time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the police station burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of the fighting in Vukovar itself, I think you've said that the resistance was very weak, almost none. However, some other witnesses testified that there was fighting for every single house. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about house-to-house combat or fighting for every house. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what HOS was?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: HOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: HOS.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that now. Today I know what HOS was. But I don't know that I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So according to you, what is HOS?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us go back in time to that period. Do you know the name of Dobroslav Paraga?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time did he have his own unit that was called HOS and were they known by the uniforms they wore, dark black?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dark black?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the acronym used to mean Croatian defence forces?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the dark black uniforms, nor did I see any HOS men in Vukovar in such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you hear about them being involved in the fighting in Vukovar, any of them?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe you said you listened to the radio. I suppose it was Radio Vukovar. Did Radio Vukovar have any programmes mentioning their involvement?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I listened to Radio Vukovar. I listened to Radio Zagreb. When the sergeant was negotiating with Raseta, that's what I heard on the radio. I don't remember about the HOS being reported as being involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your role when you accepted to be a policeman at the police station, what was it? What was your job? You said you went down to some position facing the Danube river?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That place was called Sunce, the sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think you said in all that time you didn't fire a single round?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Also you seem to have said that even before while you were with the JNA you didn't fire a single round, neither you nor any of your comrades, those four who had left?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it follows from that that you didn't fire a single bullet on other side?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was a JNA soldier I fired in the air, perhaps. But certainly not when I was with the police. I didn't even see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The rest of your colleagues, including those who were captured, did they have a combat disposition, or was perhaps some of them not assigned to anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said that Lorenc Dohanaj, myself and Zlatko Zlogledja joined the police administration and became policemen. As for the rest, none of them joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did they sleep, eat, live? With you or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they remained in the basement of the police administration building until the police station burnt down. Srecko Ravlija lost his leg; he was in the hospital. Sirkic Hamdija [phoen] was in the hospital, Kuscevic, Petar was with them at the hospital as well. Rasid Adzibegovic, I don't know where he left. I'm just telling you about myself, Zlatko and Lorenc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you yourself realised, when it became clear that Vukovar would fall, you said that you decided to go to the hospital, believing it to be the safest place?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to find shelter there at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you go and report to somebody at the hospital? Did you ask to be put on the patient list at the hospital or perhaps some other list?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the hospital because Lorenc Dohanaj stepped on a mine and it blew off his heel. We brought him to the hospital and then remained there. We didn't want to go anywhere else. I didn't report to anyone. I wasn't put on any list, either as a patient or hospital personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you have told us, prior to that you and the rest laid down your weapons. You entered the hospital unarmed and did not have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had a uniform for about 20 days or a month. I can't say with certainty. At the hospital I was in civilian clothes and without weapons. I discarded weapons at the Vukovar cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could this mean that you wanted to pass yourself off as a civilian and conceal that you had been a member of the JNA and that you wanted to leave Vukovar in this way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had no idea what was going to happen to me. I had no wish to pass myself off as anything, as somebody who fled from the JNA or did not flee from the JNA. We sought shelter at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just to clarify something for the sake of the transcript: You believed that if you went to the hospital that would save you, that was safer than anything else?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question about the hospital. I'm sure that my friends will be putting you questions about the hospital too. You said that when you left the hospital they searched you and they took your watch away and that you believed that other people were deprived of their money, valuables and so on?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I believed that, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that many witnesses testified here who had been searched, just like you were, and that all of them said that during the search they were looking for weapons and that nothing was confiscated from that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ridiculous. I don't know who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you believe that these people didn't say the truth?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ridiculous. Nobody could have entered the hospital with weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that second question, I think -- I think we agreed the questions would be put to their substance of the allegation, and I think in the first question it was put that other witnesses. But as far as this witness deciding whether he -- whether the other witnesses are telling the truth or not, I don't think that's really a position for this witness to be put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we have discussed this before. That's one step too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will not be putting evidence of these witnesses to this witness, Your Honour. I just wanted to hear his opinion and he stated that he affirmed his previous statement, so I will now turn to another topic. I thought that his answer would be different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you about how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's what everybody says when they come to testify, but it's up to us to verify this. After this you spoke about being on buses within the barracks. You described a large group which acted like a mob out of control; hitting, insulting, yelling and so on?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also mentioned an officer who got on the bus and read out some names and then that some people got off the bus and that while they were on their way to the barracks they were beaten. You explained this in detail. My question is: Did you see where these people went? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, "where did they go"? From the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see where they went after they left the yard. I just saw them going in the direction of some trucks. There were military trucks parked in the yard. Now whether they boarded them on the trucks and took them somewhere, I don't know. I just know that they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see or were you able to see these people departing in a bus?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to you that I didn't know whether they got on a bus or on a truck. I saw that they were beaten. Now what they did with them afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend about the identity of these persons who acted like a mob out of control, acting savagely around the bus, you said that a lot of them were in uniforms. My question is: Were there any people there in civilian clothes, and perhaps even some women?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where these people were from, whether they were from Vukovar or from Serbia. I have no idea where they had come from. I just saw them within the compound of the barracks. I don't know whether there were any women there. There were some women in front of barracks, but I didn't really see what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In most of your answers you said that these people wore different kinds of uniforms and that it was difficult for you to specify the number; how many JNA soldiers, how many others and so on. You said it was difficult for you to specify that. My question is this: In addition to a driver, there was a JNA soldier on each bus. I suppose I assumed that they were one of those young soldiers like yourself?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Within that mob did you see such soldiers, these young soldiers, conscripts, serving their military service, or there were none such in that mob?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't threaten us when they stood around the bus, but I'm sure that there were some JNA soldiers around the compound and also there was one JNA soldier on each bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, on each bus and in the barracks. The buses that took you to Ovcara and, in fact, en route you learned that you were going to Ovcara and you had never been there before. You described how you got there and what happened there. My question is: What happened with these buses once the people disembarked? Did the buses immediately turn and head back or did they remain there at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Five, six or seven buses arrived in a convoy at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The buses were most likely parked in front of the hangar, one behind each other?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then people got off. First one bus was emptied and then others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What happened to the buses afterwards?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: They left where?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere. Most likely they departed and left somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that was my question. Did you see, did you know where these buses went after people got off?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about where they went, because I realise that you can't possibly know that. I'm just asking you whether after people disembarked, the buses left?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a minor objection there. I think he's answered it. He said what happened to the buses afterwards and then he said they left. It just might be confusing to the witness, having the question put again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The evidence, Mr. Domazet, does appear clear. Starting at 23, about line 20, on from there. So your last question appears unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Vasic says that that's what it says in the transcript. I didn't really follow the transcript, because I had some problems, there's no transcript on my screen. I understood the witness to say that he didn't know where the buses went to, but that wasn't my question. However, I'll accept this answer and move on to something else. I apologise, Your Honour, we were trying to solve the problem with the transcript, but that's all right. I'll continue with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, in examination-in-chief you said yesterday how you saw a piece of equipment, some machinery. You said that it was a yellow bulldozer with rubber wheels?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you said it was an excavator. Do you remember testifying about this at the trial in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most likely, yes. They put questions to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that you spoke of this or not? If yes, then I will continue with my question.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they asked me, I most likely provided an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume that you don't have the transcript from the Belgrade trial in front of you. I would like to ask the usher to assist me and give you the transcript with the relevant page, and then I would like you to read it out, to see whether you remember stating this in Belgrade. The transcript is here, and then right below is the statement you gave. You may want to keep both of them. Would you please turn to page 54 of the transcript? No, I apologise, page 40. If you have found the page, towards the middle of the page, I think that your version is marked with number 1 where it says something about when they closed the hangar door. Shall I read it out and then you can confirm whether that is in your statement? Does it say so: "Once they closed the hangar door, in front of the hangar -- in front of the hangar there was an excavator, a yellow one, with rubber wheels. Not the one digging, but the one pushing, which has a fork in front of it." This is what you stated there. Did you state this or did you state what you said here?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a kind of a basket in order to carry what was being dug out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. And then after this president of the chamber asked you: "Well, does it have a plow in front of it or what?" I'm going to wait a bit for the transcript. And then you go to explain, I'm reading verbatim, and you can confirm whether I read it out correctly. "Next to that hangar was an excavator, a parked excavator. It was yellow. It had wheels, rubber wheels. It didn't have caterpillar. It had rubber wheels and a basket in front of it. It wasn't the one meant for digging." Do you see, it was the one pushing the soil, so let us repeat. You said that it had a basket, but not the one meant for digging, rather one for pushing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant. The front basket, the front shovel cannot dig, it can only push. And this is the basket shovel we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would just ask that the witness be given an opportunity to complete his answer before the question, the next question starts. I don't think it finished when Mr. Domazet had started to ask the next question. He didn't get an opportunity to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He'd had a fair go at it, Mr. Smith. I wasn't conscious of it being an unwarranted interruption, but I'm sure Mr. Domazet will continue to be careful to allow the witness to finish, just as the witness will allow Mr. Domazet to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Go ahead, please explain.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade we had a discussion with the president of the trial chamber about the front basket. It's pushing earth, not digging. It fits two cubic metres of gravel or earth or soil or whatever. I tried to explain that yesterday. That's what we had a discussion about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What I read in the first statement and after the additional question of the presiding judge, is it exactly as on the record?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree that this excavator doesn't dig at all. But the discussion was about this front basket or whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I only asked you if what is on the record is correct, your two answers in response to questions from the trial chamber?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can interpret this any way you like. I was trying to tell you what the discussion there was about. It was about the front implement that looks like a basket.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And I'm asking you about what I read out, which you had seen, not the explanation. We'll come later to the explanation.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as you talk about the front basket, then it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the front basket individually. I asked you about the entire two answers.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that you didn't read them out correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But you say that even then you testified it was an excavator of the kind that digs?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But we see here an explanation that it is the kind of machine that pushes earth, not digs. There were two discussions about this.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade they did not ask me whether the machine digs. They asked me about this front basket and what its purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the first part of the statement you gave. Are there any questions, judge's questions about the excavator, or is it your detailed story about how you left your uniform, how you got hold of civilian clothes, how you changed, how you arrived at the hangar? So it is a narrative, uninterrupted by any questions. And you come on your own to the point where they closed the door of the hangars, and outside the hangars there is a yellow excavator with rubber wheels. Not the one that -- not the one with caterpillars, with rubber wheels not the -- and the basket it had in front, not the one that digs but the one that pushes earth. And only after that the judge asked you, it had some sort of shovel underneath or in front. And then you explained again and gave this answer. You said: "The parked excavator, the yellow one with rubber wheels, has a basket in front. Not the one that digs, but the one that pushes earth." Nobody asked you about it, you said it yourself?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are reading a question from the presiding judge. He interrupted me because I had not had time to explain what -- whether there was a basket or a shovel in the back as well. And then we started this discussion about the front shovel or basket.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He did not interrupt you. It's not a deposition that is dictated. It's an audio recording that records every word during the trial. If he had really interrupted you, his question would have come before your first explanation. In your second -- after your second explanation, there were no further questions about it. It is you who continued the story on your own, saying that one soldier jump-started the machine and left somewhere. And nobody asked you anything more until the point when they asked you if there had been any other machines around and you said yes, but it wasn't a tractor, it was an excavator. Look at page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we have spent a lot of time on this, and at the moment I haven't grasped why. The witness, both in the earlier proceedings and here, seems to have been explaining that this was a piece of machinery with two operative instruments; one on the front and one on the back. The one on the back was a digger, and the one on the front, in his language, was a pusher. Whether you call it a basket, a blade or what. What is the issue that keeps you so long about this machine? The only thing he said about it, apart from its presence, was that a soldier jumped on, started it, and then left it. Nothing else said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what has been read from the transcript from Belgrade this explanation that he is giving now does not exist that there was another instrument in the back, that it was actually a digger, and that's why I wanted him to hear the quotation. However, I'm not going to dwell on this subject anymore, I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Concerning the consistency of your testimony, I would like to assess that. Yesterday in response to my various questions you quoted different numbers of tanks, I quoted you as saying there were eight, and then you said that's not true, and that you had never stated such a thing. You answered yesterday, it's page 87, you said there had never been eight and that you may have mentioned six or seven. Now I would kindly ask you to look at not this transcript but the statement you gave to OTP investigators in 1996. Would you please turn to page 2, the penultimate paragraph, and in English it is also towards the end of the second page.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does it say: "Our platoon had eight tanks and six to seven APCs."

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Our platoon," it says here. It was probably a company, not a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the Dokmanovic case where you testified as well, did you mention how many tanks there were in the possession of your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I told you that on page 611, line 22, you said your unit had had around 20 tanks at the time, and I can give you that transcript, but it's in English, and I would like to read it for the benefit of the interpreters. My friends from the Prosecution have the same transcript. And I would like to hear your answer, your explanation as to how it was possible that you mentioned 20 then, whereas yesterday you challenged that you had even mentioned eight. Not in Sremska Mitrovica. I'm speaking about the Dokmanovic trial here in the ICTY where you appeared as a witness. On page 611, 21st line, the question was: "Tanks? "Answer: Tanks. That unit of mine at that point had about 20 tanks."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm just wondering whether it could be put to the witness at which point of time that the unit had 20 tanks, whether it was at the point when they were at their position outside of Vukovar or whether it was when they were back at the barracks. It's a little bit unclear as to where that figure arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've heard that, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I've heard that. I will come back to that same page of the transcript and I will read the passage before to indicate that it was the same event. So 611, let's start from line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say: [In English] "On the 1st September, the position between Luzac and Bogdanovci, that is on the road between Vinkovci and Vukovar so we had cut that road and we dug in there with our tanks and transporters and then we were shooting at the city with everything we had available." [Interpretation] Next question: "What types of weaponry was the JNA using?" [In English] "Well, this unit of mine uses tanks, 100-millimetre tanks, and 20-millimetre transporters and PKT automatic rifles and small arms and mortars, 60 and 80 millimetres." [Interpretation] Then comes a question related to aircraft. Your response is not relevant, I believe. And after that comes this line 22 concerning tanks. And you answer: "That unit of mine at that point had about 20 tanks." So you're obviously talking about the time when you were dug in your positions after you had cut off the road?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that time concerns the period I spent in Petrovac Na Mlavi. And in relation to the other period, I never stated there had been 20 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, I'm completely at a loss. I have just read a moment ago on this page, and I don't want to go back much further, Petrovac Na Mlavi is not mentioned anywhere, we have a specific date, the 1st of September, 1991, the Bogdanovci-Vinkovci road, and you spoke about what kinds of weapons were shooting at the town, then you said on the 14th of September it was bombed by four or five planes. To the question of whether you had seen heavy artillery, you said you had seen canons and then you answered about tanks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, I think I read it out twice. I'm afraid it's quite clear that it relates to this event. The question was: "Tanks? "Answer: At that point that unit of mine had about 20 tanks." If you have no answer, I will not insist, but it's on this record.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have meant APCs and tanks in total, but it couldn't have been 20 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I really don't believe there had been 20 tanks, but I'm telling what you answered.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Petrovac Na Mlavi there were indeed 20 tanks. Maybe that's a mistake after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I should like to move on now to another subject. You said that after being taken to Belgrade, to Topcider, to the military investigations prison where you were beaten and mistreated you explained that in detail yesterday, I don't want to go on about it, but from the moment you were admitted into the military investigations prison were you beaten there and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes by reservists who would come in, but as for active duty troops, a bit, but not like in Topcider.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where was that military investigations prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the trial is taking place these days for those crimes. In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I know, the trial for those crimes is in the former courthouse.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the prison was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that's where the military investigations prison was. Was it possible for anyone other than officials, your counsel or prosecutors or whoever, was it possible for anyone to enter that building and mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reservists from Topcider who beat me was the one dispensing food at the military investigations prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Even if we admit that that is so, did you receive food there at the military investigations prison, that's why you were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all in one building, it's all within one building, the whole military investigations prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But it's also the military courthouse?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 2004 when I was in Belgrade in that cell in which I had spent four months earlier, seven months at an earlier time, I now sat as a gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I know the building you are describing, but it is not probable what you're saying; namely, that reservists bringing food would have mistreated you and beaten you -- and beat you.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were reservists, mobilised by the JNA. The reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that they brought food from Topcider to the prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were transferred to guard us. The food was cooked for us in prison. I don't know whether they actually cooked it in Topcider and then transported it to prison, but we got food in prison and they were the ones distributing food to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So you stand by your previous claim that even at the military prison you were mistreated but not by official authorities. And I suppose by that you're referring to investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the investigative judge never mistreated me. His name was Petar Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During this trial you had an attorney defending you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a court-appointed attorney, a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you referring now to the investigation or trial?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trial. But also during investigation we were offered to have defence counsel. A lady came, introduced herself. She said, I'm lawyer called such and such, court-appointed. Zlatko Zlogledja had lawyers hired by his parents. And also the Croatian side paid for some lawyers to defend us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So Zlogledja had a lawyer of his own choice hired by his family, and you had a court-appointed one?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His mother came to the trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was mistreated in a similar way just like you, if you were together in Topcider at investigative prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was mistreated to Topcider. I had to carry him to the toilet, whereas for the military investigative prison we were not there together. He was in one cell and I was in another cell. Petar Kuscevic and Samir were sent back to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You were close with him. Did he later speak to you about this?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he wasn't mistreated as badly as back in Topcider.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You or him, did you report this to your lawyers and was this ever raised in the courtroom or during investigation?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would not have been of any assistance to us or to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is: Did you raise it, did you tell this to your lawyers?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, they could see bruises on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have some five to 10 minutes more, but I think that this is our regular time for break. I will conclude shortly after we resume. I have maybe 10 questions at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will commence again at 10 minutes to 11.00. And we will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dodaj, just before the break we described what was taking place in the proceedings against you and Zlatko Zlogledja before the military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you had a court-appointed lawyer. Based on the judgement I have, it seems that her name was Zorica Petronijevic-Gajic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And based on the judgement it seems that Mr. Zlogledja was represented by two lawyers, Barovic and Tomic?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about this in detail. You were convicted for three crimes, sentenced to five years, and sent to serve your sentence in Valjevo. My only question concerning that is this: Do you know that the institution in Valjevo, the correctional centre there in the former Yugoslavia, was the one for juvenile offenders and young adults up to the age of 21 and that this is the institution where you were sent to serve your sentence?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the correctional and penal facility in Valjevo. And before Valjevo I was in the central prison in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1998 when you testified here in the Dokmanovic case you stated that you were from Kosovo and that Kosovo was under Serbian occupation. This is what you said back in 1998. Do you remember this or shall I read it out to you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely I said this. At the time I was a protected witness. Yes, I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No need to put this to you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you stated this on that occasion, that you were from Kosovo and that Kosovo was under Serbian occupation. Thank you. Am I right in saying that due to everything you experienced in 1991, 1992 and even 1993 while serving your sentence you personally felt that a great harm had been inflicted on you, both physical and mental, and that you blamed the then JNA for that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it possible that due to that your testimony, both here before this Court and some other instances where you gave evidence in a way blame the JNA and its members and that this is especially obvious in instances where you say that you were given orders to fire at Vukovar without any specific targets and then when you say that those who defended Vukovar had nothing but small arms. You also speak of the looting taking place in front of the hospital and now this piece of machinery, the backhoe loader that you described for the first time here. Can this be explained by your attitude towards the JNA and Serbia in general, especially what you said about the Serbian occupation of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm describing what I saw and what I lived through. That was done by that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you described this erroneously when you said that some ordinary soldier back on the 21st of November at 6.00 in the morning came with the news to you saying that Chetniks at Ovcara had killed 600 Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the soldier was from Cacak. And this is what he said, "Do you know what's new? Our Chetniks killed 600 Ustashas." About 600 Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is -- this was a very important matter, both back then and later, if it were indeed true?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you tell me what you stated yesterday, did you say this back in 1996 when you were interviewed by The Hague investigators?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please take a look at the statement that's before you. Take a look and tell me whether it is mentioned at all. It's not a long statement.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, in 1996 or in 1998 I came to this Court and it's natural that I didn't remember everything that had happened. You know, memories come back to you. This is an international court, after all. And when I came for the first time I was quite anxious, excited. Today I feel more comfortable. Maybe I said it and they didn't record it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you think it's possible that you stated this, but that this matter, which you yourself described as unimportant, was not recorded by the investigators who also recorded some less important things?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say this with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not so much an objection but a correction. I have the statement on the 24th of April, 1996 that the witness gave to the investigators, and just for my friends' notice, in the English version, on page 5 of 7, there is a statement to that effect. It may be a matter for re-examination, but I thought it may be important to mention that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Domazet will no doubt notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question: You went through your statement, so tell me now, is it recorded there that on the 21st in the morning a soldier from Cacak came to you bringing you the news about Chetniks killing 600 Ustashas the previous day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can find it here. It says here "major," and then I said to the investigators that this was no major, but rather an ordinary soldier. Came -- his name was not known to me, and he said that about 600 Ustashas had been killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So he's a major now?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I never said he was a major. They recorded this erroneously. This was an ordinary soldier who guarded us in Negoslavci in the basement of a Serb house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you gave your first statement prior to this in 1994 in Bjelovar, did you ever mention this?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to check that statement, I would see. And as for this one, I tell you with full certainty that this was not a major, but rather a private of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You gave your first statement in 1994 and at the time your memory was quite fresh. I would like to ask the usher to give you this statement.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that this cannot be found in your statement?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not in these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. I would like to ask the usher to bring it back to me. We will not be needing it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded with my cross-examination, and I think I was true to my word, even though I'm not a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you are neither a mathematician. You promised 10 questions, there were only 17. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the usher please give this to the witness. These are statements that have been mentioned so far and he will need to refer to them when I put some questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, good morning. My name is Borivoje Borovic. I am Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic. When you went to the front you were told that the JNA had nothing against the Croatian people; is that right? You were also told that you were going to fight Ustashas, Kurds, Albanians and so on?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please don't find my question offensive, but you are an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm not ashamed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about your friends? Were any of them Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Lorenc Dohanaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his birth place was, but in Vukovar he was from Marinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that you fired at Vukovar without any apparent reason; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please take the statement you gave to the OTP, the second one? Yes, this one, the second one. Find page 3, please, paragraph 2. I will read out what it says there, and you can confirm whether I've read it out correctly. It says: "We received no particular instructions. We were just told to fire at the town indiscriminately in the direction from which we see any fire being launched." Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that your order was this: That you would open fire indiscriminately every time you see that somebody's firing in your direction from Vukovar. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you ever fire from a tank?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not a member of a tank crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever get into a tank?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The area that you described to us in detail, the area where you were before coming to Vukovar where you spent 24 days, were you able to see from there the location of the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the police station building?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see Count Eltz's palace and did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw it. I saw that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. You will have to wait until I finish my question. So from the positions you were occupying during those four days you were not able to see that palace?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain why you said to OTP investigators that a special target that you had seen where the water-tower and the palace you have just mentioned, if you hadn't seen that palace at all looking from those positions?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the palace, but the water-tower I could see very well from our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that, you don't need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fired at it non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that that part of your statement is incorrect, that you saw the palace that was being targeted?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's written in the statement. So in the statement you gave to the OTP you said that particular targets were the palace and the water-tower. Here it is. Page 3. It's the fifth paragraph. Have you found it? Page 3, paragraph 5 reads: "Resistance in Vukovar was obviously very weak," and so on. "I saw the town was completely destroyed together with the palace and the water-tower that seemed to have been a special target or particularly targeted."

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Also in a statement that you gave to the crime investigation police in Bjelovar in 1994 on page 3, paragraph 3, English version page 3, paragraph 1, you said on the way to Dubrava you broke down all barricades and obstacles set up by the ZNG, the Home Guard Corps and the police.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't destroy them, we removed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But is it written there, "destroyed," "brought down"?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it's written. Let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I will allow you to explain. I am insisting that you describe what they looked like, those obstacles set up by the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oak logs laid across the road. Logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What did the barricades put up by the MUP look like?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written here?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we were told. Officers of the JNA told us those obstacles were put up by the ZNG, MUP and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you gave this statement in Croatia. Please don't interrupt me. You gave this statement in Bjelovar, a town in Croatia, before Croatian investigators, and there you said it was your assignment to bring down or destroy barricades and obstacles put up by the Home Guards and policemen?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this word "destroy" or "bring down." We removed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many of them did you bring down on your way to Vukovar?
